screens.title: Design Patterns for Clean Code
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn what design patterns are and why they matter for clean, maintainable code. Design patterns are reusable templates for solving recurring design problems; they are not copy-paste recipes, but structured approaches that embody principles like single responsibility, open–closed, and depending on abstractions. Practically, using a pattern communicates intent to other developers and reduces ad-hoc conditional logic and fragile coupling. For example, instead of stuffing payment logic behind many if-else branches, you can encapsulate each payment algorithm and swap them without changing the client. We'll focus on three patterns you can use today — Strategy for interchangeable algorithms, Factory Method for flexible instantiation, and Decorator for dynamic behaviour composition. Each pattern example will include a concise code excerpt and a common-mistakes checklist so you can avoid over-engineering. By the end you will be able to pick the right pattern for recurring problems, implement a clean version, and recognize when a pattern is unnecessary. Think about a recent bug you fixed — could a pattern have made that code easier to extend or test?

screens.title: What is a Design Pattern?
screens.narratorSegment: A design pattern is a general, reusable solution to a commonly occurring design problem within a particular context. It's important to emphasize that a pattern is a description of structure and intent, not runnable code you copy verbatim. Patterns capture trade-offs — they explain why a solution helps and what costs it introduces. For example, the pattern can recommend introducing an interface to decouple callers from implementations; this increases indirection, but improves testability and extensibility. You should view a pattern as a communication tool: using a named pattern like Strategy tells other developers the reason behind your structure and what they can expect when extending it. A common misconception is that patterns always make code better; in truth, prematurely applying a pattern can introduce unnecessary abstraction and cognitive load. Start with the simplest solution that works and refactor to a pattern when you see a recurring need or multiple responsibilities in a class. As a concrete example, if you find many conditional branches deciding behavior based on a type or flag, that is a sign to consider a Strategy pattern. In your next refactor, ask whether introducing the pattern reduces duplication and clarifies responsibility. What is one conditional you've recently read that could be a pattern candidate?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Patterns are design templates that document structure, intent, and trade-offs to solve recurring problems without prescribing concrete code.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › What is a Design Pattern?
Definition

Design pattern — the concept

A pattern records a tried solution, explains when to use it, and lists its trade-offs. It reduces guesswork when you face similar problems in future designs.

Intent
Why the pattern exists and the problem it addresses.
Structure
The roles and relationships the pattern suggests.
Trade-offs
What complexity the pattern adds and what it buys you.
When to avoid
If it increases indirection without solving a recurring problem.
Analogy
Think of a pattern like a modular furniture plan: it tells you how pieces fit, but you still choose materials and finish for your room.
Concrete example
When a class contains many conditionals deciding behavior, extract each behavior behind a common interface and let the client pick an implementation. That move clarifies responsibility and makes new behaviors easy to add.
Key Takeaway

Use patterns to express design intent and minimize fragile changes, but introduce them only when they solve a recurring design need.

Check your understanding
  • Does the proposed pattern reduce duplication or coupling?
  • Is the added abstraction proportional to the problem's recurrence?

screens.title: Strategy Pattern — Concept and Benefits
screens.narratorSegment: The Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable through a shared interface. The core idea is to separate the algorithm from the client that uses it. Doing so follows the Single Responsibility Principle because each strategy class focuses solely on one algorithm, and it supports the Open/Closed Principle by allowing new strategies to be added without modifying the client. A practical scenario is payment processing: instead of a single Order class filled with 'if paymentType equals' branches, you create an IPaymentStrategy interface and concrete classes such as CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment. Then the order holds a reference to the interface and uses whatever implementation it is given. Common misconceptions include thinking Strategy requires complex dependency injection. In small systems, a simple setter or constructor parameter is sufficient. Another pitfall is creating strategies for behavior that never changes — that wastes abstraction. A concrete example: you might expose a setPaymentStrategy method on an order so a UI can switch methods at checkout without altering order logic. The core takeaway is that Strategy clarifies and isolates varying behavior; ask whether behavior truly varies before extracting it into a strategy.

Architecture

Strategy pattern roles

  • Strategy interface: the abstraction all algorithms implement.
  • Concrete strategies: classes implementing the interface for each algorithm.
  • Context: holds a reference to a strategy and delegates behavior to it.
When to use
When you have multiple algorithms for the same task and you need to switch them independently of the clients.
Visual: roles and relationships
Interface
IPaymentStrategy
Concrete
CreditCardPayment
Concrete
PayPalPayment
Concrete example
Order uses an IPaymentStrategy provided at runtime. New payment methods are new strategy classes, not edits to Order.
Common mistake
Extracting a strategy before behavior actually varies can add useless indirection.
Key Takeaway

Strategy isolates varying behavior behind an interface so clients remain simple and stable while new algorithms are added as separate classes.

screens.title: Strategy Pattern — C# Example Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Now we’ll walk through a short C# example that implements the Strategy pattern. The code establishes an IPaymentStrategy interface, two concrete strategies for credit card and PayPal, and an Order context that accepts a strategy via a setter. The key idea is that Order never contains payment-specific logic; it delegates processing to the strategy. A concrete benefit is testability: tests can inject a mock strategy to verify the checkout flow without calling real payment services. Watch for two important details. First, the strategy interface should be narrow — only include operations the context needs. Second, the context should not assume internal details of concrete strategies; it treats them as black boxes. A common misconception is that strategies must be state-less. They can hold state if the algorithm requires it, but stateful strategies complicate reuse and testing, so prefer stateless or clearly documented state. As a learning exercise, rewrite the example to accept the strategy via constructor injection instead of a setter and notice how that affects the object's immutability and testing setup. Which injection style better fits your codebase's lifecycles?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Strategy — Code Walkthrough
Code excerpt (C#)

// Strategy interface
public interface IPaymentStrategy
{
  void ProcessPayment(decimal amount);
}

// Concrete strategy
public class CreditCardPayment : IPaymentStrategy
{
  public void ProcessPayment(decimal amount)
  {
    System.Console.WriteLine($"Processing credit card payment for ${amount}");
    // ... actual processing ...
  }
}

// Context
public class Order
{
  private IPaymentStrategy _paymentStrategy;
  private decimal _amount;

  public Order(decimal amount)
  {
    _amount = amount;
  }

  public void SetPaymentStrategy(IPaymentStrategy strategy)
  {
    _paymentStrategy = strategy;
  }

  public void Checkout()
  {
    if (_paymentStrategy == null) return;
    _paymentStrategy.ProcessPayment(_amount);
  }
}
This snippet shows the minimal, focused interface and a context that delegates. You can extend by adding new classes implementing IPaymentStrategy without changing Order.
Example exercise
Change the Order to accept the strategy via constructor injection and run simple unit tests that pass mock strategies to verify Checkout behavior.
Common mistake
Making the strategy interface too broad or exposing concrete details from the context couples implementations and defeats the pattern's purpose.
Key Takeaway
Keep interfaces minimal and let the context treat strategies as interchangeable black boxes to preserve extensibility.

screens.title: When Strategy is Misused
screens.narratorSegment: Strategy is powerful, but it is often misapplied. A frequent mistake is extracting a strategy for behavior that doesn't actually vary. Introducing a strategy here increases levels of indirection without solving duplication. Another misuse is making strategies responsible for unrelated tasks — that violates single responsibility and hides where state lives. Also watch for bloated interfaces that try to cover all possible future needs; broad interfaces force all strategies to implement methods they don't need. A contrasting misconception is thinking all runtime variability requires Strategy; sometimes a simple conditional with a small helper function is clearer and easier to test. To avoid these errors, ask two questions before extracting a strategy: does this behavior change frequently or across contexts, and will extracting it reduce duplication or improve testing? A practical rule of thumb: introduce Strategy when you have at least two distinct algorithms or a need to switch algorithms at runtime. As an actionable check, try the simpler refactor first, run tests, and only generalize to Strategy when duplication or conditional complexity remains. When Strategy is Misused means only extract a strategy when behavior truly varies or when it improves testability and reduces duplication.. In practical terms, common pitfalls and how to avoid over-engineering. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Strategy — Common Mistakes
Pitfall
  • Premature extraction: No real algorithm variation exists.
  • Bloated interfaces: Forcing strategies to implement unused methods.
  • Hidden responsibilities: Strategies doing unrelated work, violating SRP.
Rule of thumb
Introduce Strategy when you have two or more algorithms or need runtime swapping and test isolation.
Comparison: simple conditional vs Strategy
Simple conditional — good for one-off or very small cases. Low abstraction, easy to read.
Strategy — good when algorithms multiply or must be swapped. Higher abstraction, better extensibility and testability.
Check
If extracting Strategy increases clarity and reduces duplication, it is justified; otherwise prefer the simpler form.

screens.title: Factory Method Pattern — Concept
screens.narratorSegment: The Factory Method pattern defines an interface for creating an object, but it lets subclasses decide which concrete class to instantiate. The creator exposes a factory method that returns an abstract product; concrete creators override the factory method to produce specific product types. This pattern promotes loose coupling because the client depends on the product interface rather than specific implementations. It aligns with the Dependency Inversion Principle by making higher-level modules depend on abstractions. A typical use case is a document manager that needs to handle different document formats. The manager calls a factory method and works with the returned Document interface; concrete creators produce Word or PDF documents. A common misconception is to create factories for trivial constructors; doing so can add indirection without real benefit. Prefer Factory Method when you expect new product types and want to centralize creation logic. As an example, a DocumentCreator base class can implement shared setup and call an overridable createDocument method, so the manager logic remains unchanged as new document types arrive. Factory Method Pattern — Concept means decouple a client from concrete types by delegating instantiation to subclasses that return interface-based products.. In practical terms, defer object creation to subclasses to reduce coupling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Factory Method
Architecture

Factory Method roles

  • Product interface: the abstraction returned to the client.
  • Concrete products: implementations of the product interface.
  • Creator: declares the factory method and may contain shared logic.
  • Concrete creator: overrides factory method to return a concrete product.
Concrete example
A DocumentCreator base class calls createDocument; WordDocumentCreator and PdfDocumentCreator override createDocument to return specific product instances.
When to use
When clients should remain unaware of concrete product classes and when you want subclasses to control instantiation.
Common mistake
Using Factory Method for simple object creation that would be clearer with a constructor or simple helper function.
Key Takeaway

Factory Method centralizes and abstracts creation, letting clients work with interfaces while subclasses produce concrete instances.

screens.title: Factory Method — Java Example
screens.narratorSegment: This Java example demonstrates how a creator class defines an abstract factory method and how concrete creators produce specific products. The product interface provides open operations like open and save. Concrete implementations like WordDocument and PdfDocument satisfy the product interface and hide format-specific code. The creator's manageDocument method calls the factory method and uses the returned product without knowing its concrete type. This decouples the client from the constructor signatures and internal details of specific products. One design advantage is the ability to centralize pre- or post-creation logic in the creator while leaving instantiation choices to subclasses. A common pitfall is overusing inheritance when composition of a simple factory object would suffice. For exercise, try replacing the factory method with an injected factory object that implements the same create operation; compare both approaches and note how dependency injection can make testing and composition more flexible. Which approach simplifies extension in your codebase: subclassing creators or injecting factories? keyIdea.title: Java example insight
keyIdea.text: Creator classes can centralize shared logic while concrete creators decide which product implementation to return.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Factory Method — Code
Code excerpt (Java)

// Product interface
interface Document {
  void open();
  void save();
}

// Concrete products
class WordDocument implements Document {
  public void open() { System.out.println("Opening Word Document."); }
  public void save() { System.out.println("Saving Word Document."); }
}

class PdfDocument implements Document {
  public void open() { System.out.println("Opening PDF Document."); }
  public void save() { System.out.println("Saving PDF Document."); }
}

// Creator
abstract class DocumentCreator {
  public abstract Document createDocument();

  public void manageDocument() {
    Document doc = createDocument();
    doc.open();
    doc.save();
  }
}

// Concrete creators
class WordDocumentCreator extends DocumentCreator {
  @Override
  public Document createDocument() { return new WordDocument(); }
}

class PdfDocumentCreator extends DocumentCreator {
  @Override
  public Document createDocument() { return new PdfDocument(); }
}
This pattern keeps manager code independent of concrete document implementations and supports adding new formats through new creator classes.
Exercise
Refactor to inject a factory object implementing createDocument and compare testability to subclassing creators.
Common mistake
Overusing class inheritance for creation when a small factory object or simple constructor would be clearer.
Key Takeaway
Prefer Factory Method when you want subclasses to control instantiation while keeping client code generic over the product interface.

screens.title: Decorator Pattern — Concept
screens.narratorSegment: The Decorator pattern allows behavior to be added to an individual object dynamically, without affecting other objects from the same class. Instead of creating many subclasses to represent different combinations of behavior, you wrap the base object with decorator objects that add responsibilities. This keeps the core component clean and aligns with the Open/Closed Principle because you extend behavior through composition rather than modification. A clear example is a Coffee component: start with a SimpleCoffee object and wrap it with MilkDecorator or SugarDecorator to add cost and ingredients dynamically. A common error is misusing decorators when shared state should live in one place; decorators are best when responsibilities can be composed and remain largely independent. Decorators can be chained in different orders to produce different results, so document expected combinations and ordering semantics. When testing, treat decorators as independent units and verify the composed result. If you find yourself creating many tiny decorators that are always used together, consider bundling them into a single concrete component instead of many layers of wrappers. narration.text: The Decorator pattern allows behavior to be added to an individual object dynamically, without affecting other objects from the same class. Instead of creating many subclasses to represent different combinations of behavior, you wrap the base object with decorator objects that add responsibilities. This keeps the core component clean and aligns with the Open/Closed Principle because you extend behavior through composition rather than modification. A clear example is a Coffee component: start with a SimpleCoffee object and wrap it with MilkDecorator or SugarDecorator to add cost and ingredients dynamically. A common error is misusing decorators when shared state should live in one place; decorators are best when responsibilities can be composed and remain largely independent. Decorators can be chained in different orders to produce different results, so document expected combinations and ordering semantics. Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Decorator Pattern
Architecture

Decorator roles

  • Component interface: operations available to both base components and decorators.
  • Concrete component: the core object with base behavior.
  • Decorator: wraps a component and adds responsibilities.
Concrete example
SimpleCoffee wrapped by MilkDecorator and SugarDecorator to produce combined cost and ingredient lists without subclassing.
When to use
When you need flexible combinations of responsibilities at runtime and want to avoid many subclasses for each combination.
Common mistake
Chaining too many small decorators that are always used together; prefer grouping when appropriate.
Key Takeaway

Use Decorator to layer behavior dynamically and avoid subclass explosions, but balance granularity against practicality.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Decorator — Code Walkthrough
Code excerpt (Python)

class Coffee:
  def get_cost(self):
    return 0
  def get_ingredients(self):
    return ""

class SimpleCoffee(Coffee):
  def get_cost(self):
    return 5
  def get_ingredients(self):
    return "Coffee"

class CoffeeDecorator(Coffee):
  def __init__(self, decorated):
    self._decorated = decorated
  def get_cost(self):
    return self._decorated.get_cost()
  def get_ingredients(self):
    return self._decorated.get_ingredients()

class MilkDecorator(CoffeeDecorator):
  def get_cost(self):
    return super().get_cost() + 1.5
  def get_ingredients(self):
    return super().get_ingredients() + ", Milk"

class SugarDecorator(CoffeeDecorator):
  def get_cost(self):
    return super().get_cost() + 0.5
  def get_ingredients(self):
    return super().get_ingredients() + ", Sugar"
This demonstrates how wrapping composes behavior. You can chain decorators to build the final product dynamically at runtime.
Exercise
Create different decorator chains and assert final cost and ingredient string in unit tests to validate composition semantics.
Gotcha
The name 'decorator' appears in language features; don't confuse that syntax with the design pattern that composes objects.
Key Takeaway
Decorators let you mix responsibilities flexibly at runtime; test decorators independently and document ordering semantics.

screens.title: Choosing Between Strategy, Factory, and Decorator
screens.narratorSegment: When faced with a design decision, it's useful to map the problem to the pattern that best addresses the core issue. Use Strategy when you have multiple algorithms for the same behavior and you want to switch them or test them independently. Choose Factory Method when the main challenge is deciding which concrete type to instantiate while keeping the client decoupled from concrete classes. Use Decorator when you need to combine responsibilities at runtime without creating many subclasses. A practical comparison: if you are swapping different sorting algorithms for a collection, use Strategy; if you need to create report objects in different formats, Factory Method is appropriate; if you need to add formatting features, like pagination or headers, to a document at runtime, Decorator can compose those features. Be aware of overlaps: Factory and Strategy can be used together — a factory can produce strategy instances — and Decorator can wrap products returned by a factory. The central misconception is thinking patterns are mutually exclusive. Instead, they are composable tools. The key question to ask is: what is changing — the algorithm, the product type, or the responsibilities layered on an object?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Pattern Comparison

Which pattern fits my problem?

Strategy
Use when behavior (algorithm) changes and you want interchangeable implementations and easy testing.
Factory Method
Use when creation logic varies and clients should remain unaware of concrete product classes.
Decorator
Use when you need to compose responsibilities at runtime without subclassing for every combination.
Overlap and composition
Patterns are not exclusive. A factory may produce strategy instances, and decorators may wrap factory-produced objects. Focus on the element that changes most frequently.
Misconception to avoid
Don't apply a pattern just because it's known; apply it because it addresses the specific dimension of change in your design.

screens.title: Implement the Observer Pattern — Lab Instructions
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity asks you to implement the Observer pattern for a simple weather system. The goal is to decouple a WeatherStation subject from multiple displays so that observers receive updates without the station knowing details of each display. Start by defining an Observer interface with an update method that accepts temperature and humidity. Make CurrentConditionsDisplay and StatisticsDisplay implement this interface. Then modify WeatherStation to act as the Subject: add methods to register and remove observers, store observers in a collection, and implement notify_observers that iterates the collection and calls update. In the station's set_measurements method, call notify_observers after updating state. This exercise reinforces loose coupling and testability because you can swap display implementations without changing the WeatherStation. A common mistake is allowing observers to call back into the subject in ways that create tight coupling; keep the update contract simple and data-focused. After implementing, write a short test that registers two displays, sets measurements twice, and verifies each display observed the values. Reflect: how did decoupling improve testability and future extension? screens.title: When Patterns Become Over-engineering
screens.narratorSegment: Patterns can improve design but are not a universal solution. Over-engineering happens when you introduce abstractions that solve hypothetical future needs rather than current, recurring problems. Symptoms include long inheritance chains, many tiny classes that are always used together, and interfaces with methods no implementation needs. These signs increase cognitive load, make debugging harder, and slow down onboarding. A practical check before applying a pattern: identify the concrete pain — duplication, brittle changes, or hard-to-test code. Then estimate whether a pattern reduces that pain proportionally to the added complexity. For example, if a change requires editing five classes because behavior is scattered, a Strategy or Decorator could centralize that behavior and justify the abstraction. Conversely, if a single conditional in one small class solves the immediate need, refactor the class and monitor for repetition before extracting a full pattern. Another guideline is to favor composition over inheritance and to prefer small, well-documented abstractions. Finally, when you do introduce a pattern, keep it narrow: small interfaces, clear responsibilities, and tests that assert behavior rather than structure. Reflect: does this abstraction make the next change easier or just more indirection?

Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Design Trade-offs

Detecting over-engineering

Symptom
Many small classes always used together or interfaces with unused methods.
Test
Does the abstraction simplify unit tests and reduce the need for widespread edits?
Decision
Prefer the simplest refactor that addresses real duplication or coupling; generalize later if needed.
Practical rule
Refactor for the present pain and run tests. Introduce pattern abstractions only when repetition or brittle changes persist.
Misconception
Patterns are not badges of expertise; they are tools to reduce real complexity, not to increase abstraction for its own sake.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn what design patterns are and why they matter for clean, maintainable code. Design patterns are reusable templates for solving recurring design problems; they are not copy-paste recipes, but structured approaches that embody principles like single responsibility, open–closed, and depending on abstractions. Practically, using a pattern communicates intent to other developers and reduces ad-hoc conditional logic and fragile coupling. For example, instead of stuffing payment logic behind many if-else branches, you can encapsulate each payment algorithm and swap them without changing the client. We'll focus on three patterns you can use today — Strategy for interchangeable algorithms, Factory Method for flexible instantiation, and Decorator for dynamic behaviour composition. Each pattern example will include a concise code excerpt and a common-mistakes checklist so you can avoid over-engineering. By the end you will be able to pick the right pattern for recurring problems, implement a clean version, and recognize when a pattern is unnecessary. Think about a recent bug you fixed — could a pattern have made that code easier to extend or test?

Over the next slides you'll build a practical understanding of design patterns and how they support clean code. First, you'll recall the purpose of patterns and how they act as reusable templates for recurring design problems. Second, you'll learn to explain how individual patterns — like Strategy, Factory Method, and Decorator — help you follow principles such as single responsibility and open–closed. Third, you'll practice identifying which pattern fits common problems, so you can reduce conditional logic and coupling in real systems. Finally, you'll implement representative patterns in small, idiomatic examples so you can integrate them into everyday work. These skills matter because they change how you communicate design intent to teammates, make code easier to extend, and reduce fragile changes. A concrete example: after this chapter you'll be able to replace a monolithic report generator's if-else blocks with a strategy-based set of formatters and inject the chosen formatter without modifying the core generator. Keep in mind a common trap: patterns are tools, not goals — start simple and only introduce a pattern when it solves a recurring problem.

These additional objectives focus on application and judgment. You'll implement the three target patterns in short, idiomatic examples so you can use them in real systems. For Strategy, you'll create interchangeable algorithm classes and inject them into a context. For Factory Method, you'll build creator subclasses that decide which concrete type to instantiate. For Decorator, you'll compose responsibilities at runtime rather than relying on deep subclass trees. Equally important, you'll learn to detect misuse: when applying a pattern makes a simple solution more complex without clear benefit. A concrete exercise will ask you to implement an Observer-based event system so you can practice registering and notifying observers. Throughout, you'll learn to map problems to patterns: which pattern reduces conditionals, which reduces coupling, and which adds runtime flexibility. That mapping is a practical skill — one that helps you refactor for testability and future change. End every refactor by asking: does this simplify the current design or only add indirection?

A design pattern is a general, reusable solution to a commonly occurring design problem within a particular context. It's important to emphasize that a pattern is a description of structure and intent, not runnable code you copy verbatim. Patterns capture trade-offs — they explain why a solution helps and what costs it introduces. For example, the pattern can recommend introducing an interface to decouple callers from implementations; this increases indirection, but improves testability and extensibility. You should view a pattern as a communication tool: using a named pattern like Strategy tells other developers the reason behind your structure and what they can expect when extending it. A common misconception is that patterns always make code better; in truth, prematurely applying a pattern can introduce unnecessary abstraction and cognitive load. Start with the simplest solution that works and refactor to a pattern when you see a recurring need or multiple responsibilities in a class. As a concrete example, if you find many conditional branches deciding behavior based on a type or flag, that is a sign to consider a Strategy pattern. In your next refactor, ask whether introducing the pattern reduces duplication and clarifies responsibility. What is one conditional you've recently read that could be a pattern candidate?

The Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable through a shared interface. The core idea is to separate the algorithm from the client that uses it. Doing so follows the Single Responsibility Principle because each strategy class focuses solely on one algorithm, and it supports the Open/Closed Principle by allowing new strategies to be added without modifying the client. A practical scenario is payment processing: instead of a single Order class filled with 'if paymentType equals' branches, you create an IPaymentStrategy interface and concrete classes such as CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment. Then the order holds a reference to the interface and uses whatever implementation it is given. Common misconceptions include thinking Strategy requires complex dependency injection. In small systems, a simple setter or constructor parameter is sufficient. Another pitfall is creating strategies for behavior that never changes — that wastes abstraction. A concrete example: you might expose a setPaymentStrategy method on an order so a UI can switch methods at checkout without altering order logic. The core takeaway is that Strategy clarifies and isolates varying behavior; ask whether behavior truly varies before extracting it into a strategy.

Now we’ll walk through a short C# example that implements the Strategy pattern. The code establishes an IPaymentStrategy interface, two concrete strategies for credit card and PayPal, and an Order context that accepts a strategy via a setter. The key idea is that Order never contains payment-specific logic; it delegates processing to the strategy. A concrete benefit is testability: tests can inject a mock strategy to verify the checkout flow without calling real payment services. Watch for two important details. First, the strategy interface should be narrow — only include operations the context needs. Second, the context should not assume internal details of concrete strategies; it treats them as black boxes. A common misconception is that strategies must be state-less. They can hold state if the algorithm requires it, but stateful strategies complicate reuse and testing, so prefer stateless or clearly documented state. As a learning exercise, rewrite the example to accept the strategy via constructor injection instead of a setter and notice how that affects the object's immutability and testing setup. Which injection style better fits your codebase's lifecycles?

Strategy is powerful, but it is often misapplied. A frequent mistake is extracting a strategy for behavior that doesn't actually vary. Introducing a strategy here increases levels of indirection without solving duplication. Another misuse is making strategies responsible for unrelated tasks — that violates single responsibility and hides where state lives. Also watch for bloated interfaces that try to cover all possible future needs; broad interfaces force all strategies to implement methods they don't need. A contrasting misconception is thinking all runtime variability requires Strategy; sometimes a simple conditional with a small helper function is clearer and easier to test. To avoid these errors, ask two questions before extracting a strategy: does this behavior change frequently or across contexts, and will extracting it reduce duplication or improve testing? A practical rule of thumb: introduce Strategy when you have at least two distinct algorithms or a need to switch algorithms at runtime. As an actionable check, try the simpler refactor first, run tests, and only generalize to Strategy when duplication or conditional complexity remains. When Strategy is Misused means only extract a strategy when behavior truly varies or when it improves testability and reduces duplication.. In practical terms, common pitfalls and how to avoid over-engineering. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Factory Method pattern defines an interface for creating an object, but it lets subclasses decide which concrete class to instantiate. The creator exposes a factory method that returns an abstract product; concrete creators override the factory method to produce specific product types. This pattern promotes loose coupling because the client depends on the product interface rather than specific implementations. It aligns with the Dependency Inversion Principle by making higher-level modules depend on abstractions. A typical use case is a document manager that needs to handle different document formats. The manager calls a factory method and works with the returned Document interface; concrete creators produce Word or PDF documents. A common misconception is to create factories for trivial constructors; doing so can add indirection without real benefit. Prefer Factory Method when you expect new product types and want to centralize creation logic. As an example, a DocumentCreator base class can implement shared setup and call an overridable createDocument method, so the manager logic remains unchanged as new document types arrive. Factory Method Pattern — Concept means decouple a client from concrete types by delegating instantiation to subclasses that return interface-based products.. In practical terms, defer object creation to subclasses to reduce coupling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This Java example demonstrates how a creator class defines an abstract factory method and how concrete creators produce specific products. The product interface provides open operations like open and save. Concrete implementations like WordDocument and PdfDocument satisfy the product interface and hide format-specific code. The creator's manageDocument method calls the factory method and uses the returned product without knowing its concrete type. This decouples the client from the constructor signatures and internal details of specific products. One design advantage is the ability to centralize pre- or post-creation logic in the creator while leaving instantiation choices to subclasses. A common pitfall is overusing inheritance when composition of a simple factory object would suffice. For exercise, try replacing the factory method with an injected factory object that implements the same create operation; compare both approaches and note how dependency injection can make testing and composition more flexible. Which approach simplifies extension in your codebase: subclassing creators or injecting factories? Factory Method — Java Example means creator classes can centralize shared logic while concrete creators decide which product implementation to return.. In practical terms, see the creator, factory method, and concrete products in action. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The Decorator pattern allows behavior to be added to an individual object dynamically, without affecting other objects from the same class. Instead of creating many subclasses to represent different combinations of behavior, you wrap the base object with decorator objects that add responsibilities. This keeps the core component clean and aligns with the Open/Closed Principle because you extend behavior through composition rather than modification. A clear example is a Coffee component: start with a SimpleCoffee object and wrap it with MilkDecorator or SugarDecorator to add cost and ingredients dynamically. A common error is misusing decorators when shared state should live in one place; decorators are best when responsibilities can be composed and remain largely independent. Decorators can be chained in different orders to produce different results, so document expected combinations and ordering semantics. When testing, treat decorators as independent units and verify the composed result. If you find yourself creating many tiny decorators that are always used together, consider bundling them into a single concrete component instead of many layers of wrappers. Decorator classes accept a coffee instance, delegate base calls, and add their own cost and ingredient strings. Because decorators wrap a component, you can chain them in different orders for different results. This approach adheres to Open/Closed because adding new toppings only requires a new decorator class, not editing the base SimpleCoffee. Note an important testability point: each decorator can be tested independently by wrapping a simple stub component. When faced with a design decision, it's useful to map the problem to the pattern that best addresses the core issue. Use Strategy when you have multiple algorithms for the same behavior and you want to switch them or test them independently. Choose Factory Method when the main challenge is deciding which concrete type to instantiate while keeping the client decoupled from concrete classes. Use Decorator when you need to combine responsibilities at runtime without creating many subclasses. A practical comparison: if you are swapping different sorting algorithms for a collection, use Strategy; if you need to create report objects in different formats, Factory Method is appropriate; if you need to add formatting features, like pagination or headers, to a document at runtime, Decorator can compose those features. Be aware of overlaps: Factory and Strategy can be used together — a factory can produce strategy instances — and Decorator can wrap products returned by a factory. The central misconception is thinking patterns are mutually exclusive. Instead, they are composable tools. The key question to ask is: what is changing — the algorithm, the product type, or the responsibilities layered on an object?

Patterns can improve design but are not a universal solution. Over-engineering happens when you introduce abstractions that solve hypothetical future needs rather than current, recurring problems. Symptoms include long inheritance chains, many tiny classes that are always used together, and interfaces with methods no implementation needs. These signs increase cognitive load, make debugging harder, and slow down onboarding. A practical check before applying a pattern: identify the concrete pain — duplication, brittle changes, or hard-to-test code. Then estimate whether a pattern reduces that pain proportionally to the added complexity. For example, if a change requires editing five classes because behavior is scattered, a Strategy or Decorator could centralize that behavior and justify the abstraction. Conversely, if a single conditional in one small class solves the immediate need, refactor the class and monitor for repetition before extracting a full pattern. Another guideline is to favor composition over inheritance and to prefer small, well-documented abstractions. Finally, when you do introduce a pattern, keep it narrow: small interfaces, clear responsibilities, and tests that assert behavior rather than structure. Reflect: does this abstraction make the next change easier or just more indirection?

Let's close with the core concepts to remember. First, a design pattern is a general, reusable solution that documents intent, structure, and trade-offs. Second, the Strategy pattern encapsulates algorithms and makes them interchangeable, which reduces conditionals and supports SRP and OCP. Third, the Factory Method pattern defers object creation to subclasses so clients depend on abstractions rather than concrete types, promoting loose coupling. Each of these ideas contributes to cleaner, more maintainable code when applied judiciously. Also remember the Decorator pattern for composing behavior at runtime, the importance of avoiding premature abstraction, and the central evaluation question: does the pattern reduce duplication, improve testability, or make the code easier to evolve? Use small tests and simple refactors as your safety net, and only generalize when you see concrete, recurring design needs. Finish with three condensed reminders: First, patterns are templates — respect intent and trade-offs rather than copying code. Second, pick a pattern that addresses the primary dimension of change: algorithms, creation, or runtime responsibilities. Third, avoid premature abstraction by favoring the simplest refactor and introducing a pattern when you see real duplication or brittle change. Use small tests, narrow interfaces, and clear documentation to keep patterns maintainable.
